The course feels awkwardly structured. It begins with an introduction to C++ syntax but quickly transitions into complex topics like pointers and memory management before students have enough time to adjust. Soon after, you're assigned homework that requires using a remote server to test your code, which introduces several challenges. Without proper guidance on setting up C++ on your PC or using remote servers, you'll likely face difficulties. Learning to find memory leaks on your own is also a significant hurdle. If you're unlucky like me, debugging isn't an option due to some technical errors in the C++ setup that can't be fixed, forcing you to trace every line manually for each assignment.

These negatives highlight the course’s identity crisis—it’s caught between being a C++ course and a Data Structures and Algorithms course. This makes it awkward to teach and even more awkward for students to follow, as the pace feels erratic and unfocused. Surprisingly, the course can be very difficult for a second-year class at times, and it’s all too easy to fail if you slip up even once.

On a positive note, the TAs are helpful and willing to assist, which provides some relief. However, despite their support, the course could benefit greatly from a more cohesive structure, clearer guidance, and a more manageable pace to improve the overall learning experience.
